transcript.content: Hello, I'm glad you could make it in today. What brings you in to see me?

Well, I'm here because... well, honestly, it's been a really stressful few months at work, and I feel like I'm the only one who sees what's actually going on. I'm a transportation inspector for the county, you know, checking the buses, the transit hubs, making sure everything is up to code. And I've always been thorough. I mean, extremely thorough. That's why I won the county safety award back in November. It was a big deal, a plaque, a little ceremony, the whole nine yards. But ever since I got that award, things have just... shifted. 

Certain people at work—and I won't name names just yet, but people in the administrative office—they've been taking my inspection reports and twisting them. Like, I'll flag a minor issue with a brake line, standard procedure, and suddenly they're asking me these incredibly pointed questions about the maintenance budget and why I'm "targeting" specific garages. It's like they're trying to make me look crooked, like I'm taking kickbacks or something, which I would never do. I've got a clean record. But they keep digging, bringing up old reports from three years ago, trying to find inconsistencies. 

I tried talking to my supervisor about it, Jim, and he just brushed it off. He said, "Oh, it's just normal review, don't worry about it, budgets are tight this year." But it's not normal. You don't ask an inspector if he has a "personal vendetta" against the northside depot unless you're trying to build a case against him. I can tell, I can just feel it, there is a coordinated effort to discredit me. They want me out because I'm too good at my job, or maybe they're hiding something and they know I'll find it. But my wife said I was getting too wound up about it and made me make this appointment, so... here I am. But I'm telling you, I'm not crazy, I just know when I'm being set up.
Have you ever heard voices, whispering, or sounds when no one else was around?

Voices? No. No, absolutely not. I mean, I get why you might ask that, given the whole setup here and my wife making me come in, but no. I'm not hearing things. My hearing is actually perfectly fine, probably better than most, which you really need in my line of work. When you're out in the transit yard at, say, 11:30 at night, doing a spot check on the undercarriage of a 40-foot diesel bus, it gets pretty quiet out there. You have to listen for the hiss of a slow air leak in the brake lines, or the rattle of a loose exhaust bracket. 

So I know exactly what I'm hearing. I hear the wind, I hear the metal cooling down, I hear the traffic out on the interstate two miles away. But voices? Whispering when nobody is there? No, definitely not. If I hear whispering, it's because two of the administrative guys are literally standing by the breakroom door down the hall from my desk, and they suddenly drop their voices or stop talking the second I walk in. That’s real whispering. That's actual, physical people trying to get their story straight and figure out how to mess with my reports, not some... some imaginary voices in an empty room. Like I said before, I'm not crazy. I'm just a guy who's being targeted by very real people. So, no, no voices when no one is around. Just the normal sounds of the job.

It all started exactly when I got recognized for the county safety initiative. 

Before that? Totally fine. I was just a regular guy doing my job. I mean, I’ve been working since I got out of high school, and I never had any problems with coworkers or bosses before. I’d clock in, check the buses, clock out, go home. I trusted everybody. I thought we were all on the same team, you know? Just trying to keep the transit system running safely, making sure nobody gets hurt on a county vehicle. 

But then the county rolled out that big safety initiative—they were really cracking down on fleet maintenance standards—and I took it seriously. I was out there with my flashlight, checking the tread depth, the suspension, logging every single tiny defect, cross-referencing the maintenance logs. And they recognized me for it. They made a whole big deal about my attention to detail. 

But that’s exactly when the shift happened. About a year ago, right after that recognition. It’s like, by doing my job too well, I made the people in the administrative office look bad, or maybe they realized I was thorough enough to catch whatever they're trying to hide in the paperwork. So if you're asking if I've always been like this, always suspicious or looking over my shoulder my whole life? No. Absolutely not. It is directly tied to this past year, ever since that safety initiative recognition. Before that, everything was completely normal. I didn't have a care in the world besides doing a good day's work.
